body:
Punjab

Agricultural celebrations have strongly influenced the folk dances of Punjab.

Bhangra

Bhangra is traditionally associated with the agricultural community and the wheat harvest, particularly the festival of Baisakhi, or Vaisakhi. Historically performed mainly by men, it is now widely performed by people of different genders.

The dhol provides its characteristic energetic rhythm. Other accompanying instruments may include the tumbi, a single-string instrument, and the chimta, a metallic percussion instrument.

Giddha

Giddha is traditionally a women's folk dance of Punjab. It is performed during weddings, festivals and social gatherings. Its songs, known as boliyan, frequently express experiences of family life, relationships and society.

Rhythmic clapping is an important feature of Giddha. It should be distinguished from the traditionally male-associated harvest form of Bhangra.

Haryana

Haryana has several seasonal and festive dance forms. Phag is associated with the spring season and Holi, while Dhamal is a vigorous traditional group dance. Loor is another folk form associated with women and spring festivities.

The dhol and dholak are common sources of rhythmic accompaniment in Haryanvi folk performances.

Himachal Pradesh

Nati is among the best-known folk dances of Himachal Pradesh. Regional varieties are found in Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Kinnaur and other parts of the state.

Participants perform coordinated group movements at fairs, festivals, marriages and religious gatherings. Kullu Nati is particularly associated with the cultural celebrations of the Kullu region, including Kullu Dussehra.

Traditional instruments of the region include the dhol, nagara, flute and horns such as the narsingha or ransingha.

Uttarakhand

DanceRegion or associationIdentifying feature
ChholiyaKumaonMartial dance traditionally performed at weddings
JhoraKumaonCommunity circle dance
Pandav NrityaGarhwalRitual enactment of Mahabharata traditions
Langvir NrityaGarhwalAcrobatic performance associated with a pole

Chholiya is particularly identifiable through its traditional sword-and-shield imagery and its association with marriage processions. The dhol, damau and regional wind instruments accompany several Himalayan dance traditions.

Uttar Pradesh

Charkula is a distinctive folk dance of the Braj region, associated with Krishna-Radha traditions and celebrations following Holi. Women perform with a multi-tiered arrangement of illuminated lamps balanced on their heads.

Raas Lila is a devotional dance-drama tradition associated with the life of Krishna, especially in Mathura and Vrindavan. Nautanki, another important performing tradition of Uttar Pradesh, is principally folk theatre rather than a single dance form.

Jammu and Kashmir

Rouf, also written as Rauf or Ruf, is traditionally performed by Kashmiri women during spring and festive occasions such as Eid. Groups of dancers commonly form facing rows.

Dumhal is traditionally associated with men of the Wattal community. It is a ceremonial dance involving distinctive costumes, group singing and drum accompaniment.

Ladakh

Cham is a Buddhist ritual dance performed in Himalayan monasteries, including those of Ladakh. Masks, ceremonial costumes, drums, cymbals and horns are important elements of the tradition.

Related forms of Cham are also found in Sikkim and other Himalayan regions influenced by Tibetan Buddhism.

Prelims focus

  • Bhangra: Punjab, Baisakhi and dhol.
  • Giddha: Punjab, boliyan and clapping.
  • Nati: Himachal Pradesh, particularly the Kullu region.
  • Chholiya: Kumaon, Uttarakhand, and marriage processions.
  • Charkula: Braj region of Uttar Pradesh and illuminated lamps.
  • Trap: Rouf and Dumhal belong to Kashmir, while Nati is associated with Himachal Pradesh.

[References: Consortium for Educational Communication, Bachelor of Physical Education, Lecture 28: Indian Folk Dance; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, pp. 113 and 119-121; Himachal Tourism, Ethnic; Kullu Dussehra official website, Divine Music; Uttarakhand Judicial and Legal Academy, History of Kumaon, Folk Dances of Kumaun; Jammu and Kashmir Tourism Development Corporation, Dances of Kashmir; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Folk Dances of Northern India and the Western Himalayas

body:
Madhya Pradesh

Madhya Pradesh has important folk and tribal traditions associated with the cultural regions of Malwa, Bundelkhand and the central Indian tribal belt. Bhil, Gond and Baiga communities contribute significantly to its dance traditions.

DanceRegion or communityDistinctive association
MatkiMalwaWomen's dance involving earthen pots
JawaraBundelkhandHarvest-related celebrations and baskets of sprouts
RaiBundelkhandTraditional festive folk performance
GridaRural Madhya PradeshCelebrations associated with the growth of rabi crops
BhagoriaBhil and Bhilala communitiesTraditional Bhagoria festivities before Holi
KarmaGond, Baiga and other communitiesWorship associated with the Karam tree

Matki is associated with social occasions such as marriages. Its name refers to the earthen vessel used in the performance. Jawara, by contrast, has an agricultural association and may involve women carrying baskets of sprouted grain.

Chhattisgarh

The folk dances of Chhattisgarh reflect its agricultural society, tribal communities, pastoral occupations and devotional movements.

Panthi

Panthi is a devotional dance associated with the Satnami community and the teachings of Guru Ghasidas. It expresses religious devotion and is particularly associated with celebrations honouring Guru Ghasidas.

Raut Nacha

Raut Nacha is traditionally performed by the Raut or Yadav cowherd community. It is especially associated with Deepavali and the worship of Krishna.

Sticks, energetic group movements and rhythmic accompaniment are characteristic features. Instruments used in traditional performances include the mandar, dholak and timki.

Other important traditions

DancePrincipal association
SuaWomen's folk dance associated with a symbolic parrot and festive occasions
SailaTraditional tribal stick dance
KarmaTribal agricultural and religious celebrations
Gaur MariaMaria Gond communities of Bastar
GediTraditional dancing using stilts

Pandavani is another important cultural tradition of Chhattisgarh, but it is primarily a musical storytelling form based on the Mahabharata. It should not be classified simply as a folk dance.

Karma as a shared regional tradition

Karma, also called Karam, is a major example of a dance and festival tradition shared across state boundaries. It is practised by various communities in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha and Bihar.

The Karam tree or its branch holds ritual significance. The celebration is connected with agricultural well-being, prosperity and community life. Men and women may participate in group dances accompanied by songs and drums.

Prelims focus

  • Matki: Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh.
  • Bhagoria: Bhil and Bhilala communities of Madhya Pradesh.
  • Panthi: Satnami community and Guru Ghasidas.
  • Raut Nacha: Chhattisgarh, cowherd communities and Deepavali.
  • Gaur Maria: Bastar region.
  • Trap: Karma is not exclusive to a single state.

[References: Ministry of Culture, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 85, 3 February 2020, Annexure on Folk Cultures of Madhya Pradesh and Bihar; Consortium for Educational Communication, Lecture 28: Indian Folk Dance; District Durg, Government of Chhattisgarh, cultural traditions; Incredible India, Diwali in Chhattisgarh and Shivrinarayan Mela; Jharkhand Tourism, Art and Culture: Karma; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Five states connect equally to Karma or Karam, with a shared basis in the Karam tree, agricultural prosperity, group dancing, songs and drums.
pictures.caption: Karma as a shared regional tradition.

title: Folk and Tribal Dances of Central India

body:
Bihar

Jat-Jatin

Jat-Jatin is associated particularly with the Mithila and Koshi regions of northern Bihar. It is traditionally performed during the monsoon season.

The songs and enactments portray the relationship between Jat and Jatin, including separation, migration for employment, affection and the hardships of rural life. Different performance traditions may represent the characters through paired dancers or groups of women.

Jhijhiya

Jhijhiya is a ritual folk dance associated with women in Bihar, particularly the Mithila region. One well-known festive form involves dancing with perforated earthen pots containing lamps during Navratri.

Regional descriptions also associate Jhijhiya songs with prayers for rainfall and agricultural prosperity.

Jharni and other traditions

Jharni is performed by members of the Julaha community during Muharram. Split bamboo sticks are used to produce a rhythmic accompaniment.

Domkach is associated with marriage celebrations in Bihar and neighbouring Jharkhand. Jhumar and Jhumari are also important regional traditions.

Jharkhand

The dances of Jharkhand are closely connected with tribal festivals, seasonal changes and village life. Different communities maintain distinctive songs and performance traditions.

Dance or traditionPrincipal association
KarmaKaram festival, prosperity and collective worship
JhumarRegional festive and community dance
Sarhul dancesSpring festival and worship connected with nature
PaikaTraditional martial dance
DomkachMarriage celebrations
Seraikella ChhauRegional masked style of Chhau

The mandar, a traditional drum, is an important source of rhythmic accompaniment in many eastern Indian tribal dance traditions. Other instruments and singing patterns differ according to the community and occasion.

West Bengal

Dance or traditionIdentifying association
Purulia ChhauLarge decorative masks and mythological themes
GambhiraMalda region, Shiva-related festivities and social themes
Santhal danceSanthal community and seasonal celebrations
TusuHarvest-season folk tradition
RaibensheTraditional martial folk dance

Gambhira combines songs, dance, religious themes and commentary on social life. The dhak, a large traditional drum, accompanies several of its performances.

The Santhal community is distributed across several states, including West Bengal, Jharkhand and Odisha. Santhal dances therefore cannot be restricted to West Bengal alone.

Odisha

Odisha's folk and tribal dance traditions are particularly diverse in its western districts and tribal regions.

DanceRegion or associationFeature
DalkhaiWestern OdishaFestive group dance accompanied by Dalkhai songs
GhumuraKalahandiDistinctive Ghumura drum
DhemsaTribal regions of southern OdishaCoordinated group dancing
KarmaWestern Odisha and tribal communitiesKaram worship and collective celebrations
Mayurbhanj ChhauMayurbhanj districtUnmasked Chhau tradition

Dalkhai is particularly associated with festivals such as Dussehra and Bhai Jiuntia. Its accompaniment may include the dhol, nisan, tasa, timki and muhuri.

Ghumura takes its name from a traditional drum and is strongly associated with the Kalahandi region. It is performed during occasions such as Nuakhai, a harvest festival, and Dussehra.

Prelims focus

  • Jat-Jatin: Mithila and Koshi regions of Bihar.
  • Jharni: Bihar and Muharram.
  • Gambhira: Malda, West Bengal.
  • Dalkhai: western Odisha and festive celebrations.
  • Ghumura: Kalahandi, Odisha, and the Ghumura drum.
  • Trap: Dhemsa or Dhimsa is found in both Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.

[References: Bihar Foundation, Music and Dance; Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha state cultural profiles; Jharkhand Tourism, Art and Culture: Karma; Government of West Bengal, Music and Dance; District Sambalpur, Culture and Heritage; District Kalahandi, Art Forms; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Lok Sabha Starred Question 107, 11 December 2023, Annexure II; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Folk and Tribal Dances of Eastern India

body:
Nature and cultural background

Chhau is a traditional dance form of eastern India that combines elements of martial traditions, folk culture, dramatic storytelling and religious themes.

It is particularly associated with the adjoining cultural regions of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha. Tribal communities and other local groups have contributed to the development and preservation of its regional styles.

Performances depict stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, local mythology and folklore. Chhau is closely associated with Chaitra Parva, a spring festival observed during the Hindu month of Chaitra.

The 3 regional styles

StyleStateUse of masks
Seraikella ChhauJharkhandUses masks
Purulia ChhauWest BengalUses masks
Mayurbhanj ChhauOdishaDoes not traditionally use masks

The masks of Seraikella Chhau are generally more restrained in appearance, whereas Purulia Chhau is noted for its large, colourful masks and elaborate headgear.

Mayurbhanj Chhau is distinguished by the absence of masks. This is one of the most important identifying differences among the 3 regional traditions.

Music and instruments

Chhau is accompanied by traditional percussion instruments and melodic wind instruments. The dhol and dhamsa provide powerful rhythmic accompaniment.

Melodic accompaniment is provided by reed instruments such as the mohuri or shehnai. These instruments support the dramatic nature of the performance.

Chhau and mask-making traditions

The use of masks in Seraikella and Purulia Chhau has supported specialised traditions of mask-making. In West Bengal, Charida village in Purulia district is particularly associated with Chhau masks.

The masks represent characters from religious stories, folklore and mythological narratives. They are an important part of the cultural identity of the masked styles.

UNESCO recognition

Chhau dance was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010, under Decision 5.COM 6.15.

The recognised cultural element includes the Chhau tradition with its regional varieties. The inscription is not restricted to the masked forms alone.

Chhau is sometimes described as a semi-classical dance tradition because it combines established artistic conventions with regional folk and martial elements. It is not one of the conventional 8 Indian classical dance forms.

Prelims focus

  • Seraikella Chhau: Jharkhand.
  • Purulia Chhau: West Bengal.
  • Mayurbhanj Chhau: Odisha.
  • Chaitra Parva: spring festival associated with Chhau.
  • UNESCO inscription: 2010.
  • Trap: Mayurbhanj Chhau traditionally does not use masks.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10: Theatre Crafts, pp. 113-115; UNESCO, Chhau Dance, nomination file 00337 and Decision 5.COM 6.15; Government of West Bengal, Music and Dance. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Chhau performers compared: Seraikella wears a restrained mask, Purulia a colourful mask with elaborate headgear, and Mayurbhanj has an uncovered face.
pictures.caption: The three regional styles of Chhau.
